questions.q: Why does the pipeline track a set of processed incident IDs in processed_findings.json?
options: To avoid re-processing and re-containing the same incident every time the poll loop runs
Because Sentinel deletes incidents older than one poll interval
To satisfy a compliance requirement unrelated to the pipeline's logic
Because graph_client requires a local cache of every user in the tenant
questions.explain: Without tracking which incidents have already been handled, a loop that re-queries a rolling time window would reprocess -- and potentially re-contain -- the same finding on every pass.

questions.q: What does enrich_incident() do, and what does it deliberately NOT do?
options: It revokes the user's session; it does not log the action
It pulls recent sign-ins and threat-intel hits for the flagged user; it never changes any account state
It disables the account and then checks whether that was the right call
It only formats a Slack message; it performs no API calls
questions.explain: enrich_incident() is read-only lookup work -- sign-ins and IP reputation -- with no side effects on the user's account.

questions.q: Why does propose_containment() return a plain dict instead of calling the Graph API directly?
options: Dicts execute faster than API calls in Python
Because the Graph API does not accept Python dicts as input
Because Sentinel incidents cannot be serialized any other way
So the proposed action can be inspected, logged, posted for approval, or unit tested before anything real happens
questions.explain: Building the action as inspectable data first is what makes it possible to gate, log, or test the decision before any account is actually touched.

questions.q: In execute_containment(), what happens if dry_run=False is passed but approved_by is left as None?
options: The function executes the action anyway, assuming default approval
The function silently defaults back to dry_run=True
The function raises a RuntimeError and refuses to run unattended
The function retries the API call three times before failing
questions.explain: Turning off dry_run alone isn't enough -- execute_containment() still refuses to act without an explicit approved_by value, a second independent guardrail.

questions.q: Why is dry_run=True chosen as the function's default value rather than an optional flag someone passes explicitly?
options: Default values run faster in Python than required parameters
So a script invoked without thinking carefully about the flag logs its intended action instead of silently taking it
Because Graph API calls fail by default unless explicitly overridden
There is no real difference; it is a style preference only
questions.explain: Making the safe behavior the default means a careless or rushed invocation fails safe into logging, not into an unreviewed real action.
